title: UPDATE: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Says Memory Chip Glut Unlikely by 2029
summary:
The chief executive of Nvidia disagreed with forecasts that new chip production will lead to a memory sector price war, stating that the components are in perpetual demand. Jensen Huang told CNBC that a surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029, rejecting a Korean newspaper's prediction that the market would become a "red ocean" of oversupply. Huang cited the increasing use of LPDDR memory in data centers as a primary driver of long-term demand.

The outlook comes as Micron faces a strike on Thursday by the union representing its Taoyuan workers in Taiwan, who are demanding a permanent payment system based on 15% of the company's operating profit. Market tension is further highlighted by some U.S. PC builders reporting that DDR5 prices rose 10% to 15% this week, and a $95B AI server backlog at Dell continues to constrain deliveries.

selectedTweets.text:
$NVDA Jensen Huang: Surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029. 

The CNBC question referenced a Korean newspaper opinion on $KOSPI / Samsung / SK Hynix that predicted "new supply will leave the memory sector a red ocean in 2029."

"One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it", Jensen said, citing LPDDR usage in DCs.  And responded "I don't think so" in terms of possibilities of oversupply in 2029. 

Just my personal opinion, Nvidia probably has the most visibility in the entire industry. 

Especially around supply procurement and emerging capacity, given they're the ones leading all the architectural shifts. 

On durability, you have Samsung already allocated majority of capacity into 2031 from SED and hyperscalers like $GOOGL are already reportedly securing memory LTAs into 2035 from KeyBanc. 

Yet there's endless "it's all over" sentiment on memory now. I'd probably trust Jensen's opinion here.

selectedTweets.bestBit: A PC builder in the United States says its supplier raised DDR5 prices another 10% to 15% this week
selectedTweets.text:
Memory prices are still going UP, and suppliers are now tearing up cheap orders.

A PC builder in the United States says its supplier raised DDR5 prices another 10% to 15% this week.

The supplier also canceled every open order that had not shipped yet, so customers have to order again at the new, higher price.

TrendForce still expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% this quarter, after roughly 80% in the second quarter and 40% in the third.

According to Taiwanese media, some smartphone makers are now downgrading their screens just to offset the cost of memory.

The market keeps treating slower price growth like a price crash but is not.

Prices are still climbing from record highs, and that is great for $MU, Samsung and SK Hynix.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Michael Dell just told the Wall Street Journal that the memory crunch is going to get WORSE.

On CNBC this week he said supply and demand get worse next year, and when asked about memory he called it "maybe a four year problem because there's just not enough supply."

His reasoning is that a new chip fab takes about four years to build, so the capacity being planned today may not produce anything until 2029 or 2030.

That is a STRUCTURAL shortage, and it is exactly what Samsung, SK Hynix and $MU want to hear after the brutal selloff in memory stocks this week.

The more interesting part is how $DELL plans to survive if the AI boom ever busts.

Dell builds just in time, so it isn't sitting on a mountain of inventory or debt like a lot of AI infrastructure players, and the WSJ says that gives it a CUSHION if demand collapses.

One of the biggest buyers of memory in the world is telling you the shortage isn't close to over.

selectedTweets.bestBit: the union representing Micron's Taoyuan workers says it will strike on Thursday
selectedTweets.text:
$MU workers in Taiwan are about to WALK OUT.

According to Reuters, the union representing Micron's Taoyuan workers says it will strike on Thursday, the same day the company sits down for mediation with a second union at its Taichung operations.

This is not a small site because taiwan is where $MU makes a huge share of its DRAM and HBM, the exact chips every AI server is fighting over right now.

The dispute is about money because the union wants a permanent system that pays employees 15% of Micron's operating profit, instead of the one time bonus Micron offered for fiscal 2026.

And Micron just made $99.34 billion in operating income last fiscal year, so you can see why workers feel they deserve a bigger slice.

The Taoyuan union has not said how long the strike will last and the much larger Taichung union, which covers most of Micron's roughly 15,000 Taiwan employees, has not voted on a strike yet.

Micron has already said it has sold out the 2027 capacity at its new Taichung facility, so even a short disruption lands on a market with almost no slack.

I don't expect this to shut down production but in a memory market this TIGHT, even the risk of lost output matters for $MU, Samsung and SK Hynix.
